Empirical Research Plan – Foster‐Care Placements in Illinois, 1990–2001  

-------------------------------------------------------------

1. Identification Strategy  
   • Method: Two–stage least squares (2SLS) / instrumental variables (IV).  
   • Instrument: The investigator’s “placement propensity” – the leave-one-out mean removal rate in the investigator’s other cases, measured within office × calendar‐quarter (or month) to preserve common shocks.  
   • Justification:  
     – Treatment (actual foster-care removal) is highly endogenous to child/family risk.  
     – Investigators are assigned quasi-randomly from fixed rotation lists; conditional on office × time, the investigator’s identity is as good as random.  
     – Investigators differ systematically in aggressiveness; this generates exogenous variation in treatment intensity that is plausibly unrelated to any single child’s unobservables except through removal.  
   • Estimand: The local average treatment effect (LATE) for children whose placement status is changed by being seen by a marginally more or less aggressive investigator (the “marginal child”).  

2. Treatment and Control  
   • Treatment variable (D): Indicator equal to 1 if the child is removed from the home within seven days of the initial investigation and placed into foster care; 0 otherwise.  
   • Control group: Children investigated and NOT removed (they either remain at home with or without services).  
   • Timing: Event date t = date of first investigation visit. Outcomes measured in adolescence and adulthood (e.g., delinquency at ages 13-17, employment and earnings at ages 18-25). No staggered adoption problem because treatment is decided immediately.  
   • No running variable/cutoff (not RDD).  

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
   A1. Relevance – The instrument strongly predicts foster-care placement.  
       • Plausibility: Empirically testable in first stage; historical data typically show 10- to 20-ppt differences across investigators.  
   A2. Independence (as-good-as-random assignment) – Conditional on office × time fixed effects (and pre-case covariates), investigator aggressiveness is independent of unobserved determinants of later outcomes.  
       • Plausibility: Assignment is mechanical rotation; we can check covariate balance across instrument quantiles.  
   A3. Exclusion – Investigator aggressiveness influences later outcomes only through the removal decision, not via other channels (e.g., differential referral to services).  
       • Plausibility: Investigators have limited scope beyond the removal decision; we will explore this by showing negligible effects on immediate in-home services among non-removed children.  
   A4. Monotonicity – No child would be removed by a lenient investigator but kept at home by a strict one (no “defiers”).  
       • Plausibility: Because aggressiveness raises (never lowers) the probability of removal, this assumption is credible.  
   A5. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA) – One child’s assignment to a strict investigator does not affect another child’s outcome (no spillovers within families handled separately).  
       • Plausibility: We restrict to first investigation per child and cluster s.e. at family × office level.  

4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  
   1. Non-random assignment (violation of A2).  
      • Balance tests of baseline risk factors versus instrument bins; include rich controls (age, race, prior hotline calls).  
      • Add office × day-of-week × shift fixed effects; drop offices/times where rotation not strictly followed.  
   2. Exclusion violation through differential service referrals.  
      • Document service take-up among non-removed children by instrument strength; include “in-home service” indicator as control; show results robust to excluding cases that received additional services.  
   3. Measurement error in instrument (propensity imprecise for low-case investigators).  
      • Use leave-out mean over full sample horizon; drop investigators with <20 historical cases; weight 2SLS by inverse of first-stage variance (Angrist–Krueger method); show results using jackknife IV.  

5. R Code Outline
```r
# 0. Packages ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # fast IV estimators
library(modelsummary) # neat tables

# 1. Load Data --------------------------------------------------------------
cases <- fread("dcfs_cases_1990_2001.csv")          # one row per investigated child
outcomes <- fread("linked_longrun_outcomes.csv")    # adult/teen outcomes

# 2. Merge & Keep Marginal Sample ------------------------------------------
df <- merge(cases, outcomes, by = "child_id")

# Def.: marginal if allegation not extremely severe/benign (provided flag)
df <- df[marginal_case == 1]

# 3. Construct Instrument ---------------------------------------------------
# Leave-one-out removal rate by investigator within office-quarter
df[, quarter := paste0(year(inv_date), "-Q", quarter(inv_date))]
df[, removal_rate := mean(removed), by = .(investigator_id, quarter)]
df[, n_cases_inv_q := .N,         by = .(investigator_id, quarter)]

# Leave-one-out: subtract own case
df[, instr := (removal_rate*n_cases_inv_q - removed)/(pmax(n_cases_inv_q - 1,1))]

# Drop investigators with small history
df <- df[n_cases_inv_q >= 20]

# 4. Main 2SLS Specification -----------------------------------------------
# Example outcome: ever arrested age 13-17
spec_main <- feols(arrest_13_17 ~ treat_removed | 
                   0 | instr ~ treat_removed |
                   office_id + quarter, 
                   data = df, weights = ~case_weight)

# Show results
etable(spec_main, se = "cluster", cluster = "investigator_id")

# 5. Robustness: instrument defined at investigator-year -------------------
df[, yr := year(inv_date)]
df[, inv_year_rate := mean(removed), by = .(investigator_id, yr)]
df[, instr_year := (inv_year_rate*.N - removed)/(pmax(.N-1,1)), by = .(investigator_id, yr)]

spec_rb <- feols(arrest_13_17 ~ treat_removed | instr_year |
                 office_id + yr, data = df, cluster = "investigator_id")
etable(list(main = spec_main, year_def = spec_rb))

# 6. Additional robustness: add child covariates ---------------------------
covars <- c("child_age", "child_gender", "race_black", "prior_hotline_calls")
form <- reformulate(c(covars, "treat_removed"), response = "arrest_13_17")
spec_cov <- feols(as.formula(form) | 
                  instr ~ treat_removed | 
                  office_id + quarter, data = df)
etable(list(main = spec_main, with_cov = spec_cov))
```

6. Expected Results  
   Prior from psychology and existing quasi-experimental evidence suggests foster-care removal often harms marginal children relative to staying at home (loss of kin networks, instability). I expect:  
     • Juvenile arrests: +5 to +10 percentage points (baseline ≈ 20%).  
     • Teen motherhood: +3 p.p. for girls (baseline ≈ 10%).  
     • Adult annual earnings (age 24-26): –$2,000 (≈ −10%).  

   Magnitudes reflect LATE for children on the margin of removal, not the average foster child.  

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)  
   C1. Relevance (first-stage F-stat > 10) ................................. 1  
   C2. Independence / random assignment of instrument ...................... 0.8  
   C3. Exclusion (no direct effect beyond removal) .......................... 0.6  
   C4. Monotonicity (no defiers) ........................................... 0.9  
   C5. SUTVA / no spillovers ............................................... 0.8  
   Overall: 4.1 / 5 – credible but must document balance and exclusion rigorously.
